claim: Notch signaling is an integral part of the Wnt and Fgf signaling feedback loop coordinating cell migration and the self-organization of rosette-shaped sensory organs in the zebrafish lateral line system.
source: We demonstrate that Notch signaling is an integral part of the Wnt and Fgf signaling feedback loop coordinating cell migration and the self-organization of rosette-shaped sensory organs in the zebrafish lateral line system.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including signaling pathway analyses and genetic manipulations.

claim: Notch signaling acts downstream of Fgf signaling to inhibit hair cell differentiation.
source: We show that Notch signaling acts downstream of Fgf signaling to not only inhibit hair cell differentiation but also to induce and maintain stable epithelial rosettes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that Fgf signaling is required for Notch activation, and that Notch inhibits atoh1a expression which is required for hair cell differentiation.

claim: Notch signaling acts downstream of Fgf signaling to induce and maintain stable epithelial rosettes.
source: We show that Notch signaling acts downstream of Fgf signaling to not only inhibit hair cell differentiation but also to induce and maintain stable epithelial rosettes.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that NICD can induce rosettes even in the absence of Fgf signaling, and that Notch acts downstream of Fgf in the signaling cascade.

claim: Ectopic Notch expression causes a significant increase in organ size independently of proliferation.
source: Ectopic Notch expression causes a significant increase in organ size independently of proliferation and the Hippo pathway.
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation assays showing decreased proliferation in NICD neuromasts, and cell cycle inhibition experiments showing that NICD neuromast size is not reduced by blocking proliferation.

claim: Ectopic Notch expression causes a significant increase in organ size independently of the Hippo pathway.
source: Ectopic Notch expression causes a significant increase in organ size independently of proliferation and the Hippo pathway.
evidence: Demonstrated by yap1 morpholino experiments showing that yap1 downregulation does not rescue neuromast size in NICD embryos to wildtype levels.

claim: Notch signaling induces apical junctional complex genes that regulate cell adhesion and apical constriction.
source: Transplantation and RNASeq analyses revealed that Notch signaling induces apical junctional complex genes that regulate cell adhesion and apical constriction.
evidence: Supported by RNASeq data showing upregulation of adherens junction and tight junction genes, and GO term analysis identifying 'apical junction complex' as an enriched cellular component.

claim: In the absence of patterning cues normally provided by a Wnt/Fgf signaling system, rosettes still self-organize in the presence of Notch signaling.
source: Our analysis also demonstrates that in the absence of patterning cues normally provided by a Wnt/Fgf signaling system, rosettes still self-organize in the presence of Notch signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that NICD primordia form proneuromasts even when treated with Fgfr1 inhibitors or MAPK inhibitors.

claim: The zebrafish lateral line is a powerful model to study sensory organ morphogenesis because it develops superficially in the skin and is amenable to experimental manipulation and in vivo imaging.
source: The zebrafish lateral line is a powerful model to study sensory organ morphogenesis, as it develops superficially in the skin and is amenable to experimental manipulation and in vivo imaging.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the zebrafish lateral line system as a model organism.

claim: The lateral line is a sensory system for the detection of water movements.
source: The lateral line is a sensory system for the detection of water movements and consists of rosette-shaped sensory organs (neuromasts) that are arranged in lines along the body of the animal.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the lateral line system.

claim: The lateral line consists of rosette-shaped sensory organs (neuromasts) that are arranged in lines along the body of the animal.
source: The lateral line is a sensory system for the detection of water movements and consists of rosette-shaped sensory organs (neuromasts) that are arranged in lines along the body of the animal.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the anatomical organization of the lateral line system.

claim: Each neuromast is composed of sensory hair cells surrounded by support cells.
source: Each neuromast is composed of sensory hair cells surrounded by support cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuromast cellular composition.

claim: Lateral line hair cells are homologous to vertebrate inner ear hair cells.
source: Lateral line hair cells are homologous to vertebrate inner ear hair cells and are specified by the same molecules (Nicolson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Lateral line hair cells are specified by the same molecules as vertebrate inner ear hair cells.
source: Lateral line hair cells are homologous to vertebrate inner ear hair cells and are specified by the same molecules (Nicolson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The lateral line system on the trunk develops from an ectodermal placode posterior to the ear that migrates to the tail tip.
source: The lateral line system on the trunk develops from an ectodermal placode posterior to the ear that migrates to the tail tip.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lateral line development.

claim: The migrating primordium periodically deposits clusters of cells that mature into neuromasts, thus forming a line of sensory organs.
source: The migrating placode (now called primordium) periodically deposits clusters of cells that mature into neuromasts, thus forming a line of sensory organs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lateral line development.

claim: The migrating primordium consists of a mesenchymal leading region and a trailing region in which cells apically-basally polarize and then apically constrict to form garlic bulb/rosette-shaped proneuromasts.
source: This migrating primordium consists of a mesenchymal leading region and a trailing region in which cells apically-basally polarize and then apically constrict to form garlic bulb/rosette-shaped proneuromasts (reviewed in [Harding et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The two domains of the primordium are maintained by a feedback mechanism between the Wnt and Fgf pathways.
source: The two domains are maintained by a feedback mechanism between the Wnt and Fgf pathways (Aman and Piotrowski, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Activation of the Wnt pathway in the leading region induces Fgf ligands that activate the Fgf pathway in the trailing region.
source: Activation of the Wnt pathway in the leading region induces Fgf ligands that activate the Fgf pathway in the trailing region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Wnt-Fgf signaling feedback loop in the lateral line.

claim: Fgf ligand expression is uniform in the leading region but then becomes restricted to one central cell as organs (proneuromasts) begin to form.
source: Fgf ligand expression is uniform in the leading region but then becomes restricted to one central cell as organs (proneuromasts) begin to form.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Fgf ligand expression patterns during proneuromast formation.

claim: Fgf ligand expression by a central proneuromast cell that activates Fgf signaling in surrounding cells is crucial for proneuromast formation and maintenance.
source: Fgf ligand expression by a central proneuromast cell that activates Fgf signaling in surrounding cells is crucial for proneuromast formation and maintenance (Durdu et al., 2014; Ernst et al., 2012; Harding and Nechiporuk, 2012; Lecaudey et al., 2008; Nechiporuk and Raible, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Fgfr-Ras-Mapk signaling is thought to directly induce apical constriction and rosette formation via the activation of the actin-binding protein shroom3.
source: Fgfr-Ras-Mapk signaling is thought to directly induce apical constriction and rosette formation via the activation of the actin-binding protein shroom3.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature that the authors later challenge with their own data.

claim: shroom3 leads to apical localization of Rock2a kinase that phosphorylates non-muscle myosin II (pNMII) driving actomyosin constriction.
source: shroom3 leads to apical localization of Rock2a kinase that phosphorylates non-muscle myosin II (pNMII) driving actomyosin constriction (Ernst et al., 2012; Harding and Nechiporuk, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Of all the mutants/manipulations thus far analyzed that affect lateral line development only very few lead to an increase in organ size.
source: Of all the mutants/manipulations thus far analyzed that affect lateral line development only very few lead to an increase in organ size.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the literature and provides context for the novelty of the findings.

claim: The only manipulation described that causes an increase in neuromast size is the upregulation of Wnt signaling.
source: The only manipulation described that causes an increase in neuromast size is the upregulation of Wnt signaling, while the size of the primordium increases after inhibition of the Hippo pathway member amotl2a (Agarwala et al., 2015; Head et al., 2013; Wada et al., 2013; Wada and Kawakami, 2015; Jacques et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The size of the primordium increases after inhibition of the Hippo pathway member amotl2a.
source: The only manipulation described that causes an increase in neuromast size is the upregulation of Wnt signaling, while the size of the primordium increases after inhibition of the Hippo pathway member amotl2a (Agarwala et al., 2015; Head et al., 2013; Wada et al., 2013; Wada and Kawakami, 2015; Jacques et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Hippo pathway controls organ size via a kinase cascade that leads to the phosphorylation and degradation of the transcriptional co-activators Yap/Taz.
source: The Hippo pathway controls organ size via a kinase cascade that leads to the phosphorylation and degradation of the transcriptional co-activators Yap/Taz (Sun and Irvine, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: In the absence of Hippo pathway activation, Yap/Taz are translocated to the nucleus where they activate proliferation and survival genes.
source: In the absence of pathway activation, Yap/Taz are translocated to the nucleus where they activate proliferation and survival genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Yap/Taz function in the Hippo pathway.

claim: The Wnt pathway affects organ size via controlling proliferation, which, at least partially, is regulated by amotl2a.
source: The Wnt pathway affects organ size via controlling proliferation, which, at least partially, is regulated by amotl2a (Agarwala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of the transcriptional co-activator yap1 rescues the amotl2a overproliferation phenotype but does not interact with the Wnt pathway.
source: In contrast, loss of the transcriptional co-activator yap1 rescues the amotl2a overproliferation phenotype but does not interact with the Wnt pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about published findings that provides context for the current study.

claim: The upregulation of Notch signaling by overexpression of the Notch1a intracellular domain (ICD; NICD) in the primordium leads to a significant increase in neuromast size.
source: Here we describe how the upregulation of Notch signaling by overexpression of the Notch1a intracellular domain (ICD; NICD, [Scheer and Campos-Ortega, 1999]) in the primordium, leads to a significant increase in neuromast size.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing increased neuromast size in NICD embryos.

claim: The increased neuromast size in both Notch and Wnt overexpressing embryos is yap1-independent.
source: The increased neuromast size in both Notch and Wnt overexpressing embryos is yap1-independent, and in case of NICD the organ size increase is even proliferation-independent.
evidence: This is supported by yap1 morpholino experiments showing that yap1 downregulation does not rescue neuromast size to wildtype levels.

claim: In the case of NICD the organ size increase is proliferation-independent.
source: The increased neuromast size in both Notch and Wnt overexpressing embryos is yap1-independent, and in case of NICD the organ size increase is even proliferation-independent.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation assays and cell cycle inhibition experiments.

claim: Apical constriction is driven by cortical tension-generating actomyosin contractions that are transmitted to neighboring cells via apically localized cadherins.
source: Apical constriction is driven by cortical tension-generating actomyosin contractions that are transmitted to neighboring cells via apically localized cadherins (reviewed in [Heisenberg and Bellaïche, 2013; Martin et al., 2009; Pilot and Lecuit, 2005; Schwayer et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of apical constriction, supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Fgf-dependent Notch signaling cell-autonomously upregulates adherens and tight junction molecules downstream of Fgf signaling.
source: We demonstrate that Fgf-dependent Notch signaling cell-autonomously, and downstream of Fgf signaling upregulates adherens and tight junction molecules.
evidence: This is supported by RNASeq data, in situ hybridization, and transplantation experiments.

claim: Adherens and tight junction molecules together form an apical junctional complex associated with a circumferential actomyosin belt.
source: These molecules together form an apical junctional complex associated with a circumferential actomyosin belt (Niessen, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of apical junctional complexes, supported by citation.

claim: Notch signaling increases organ size independently of proliferation by coordinating actomyosin activation and cell adhesion.
source: Thus, Notch signaling increases organ size independently of proliferation by coordinating actomyosin activation and cell adhesion.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including proliferation assays, RNASeq, and cell adhesion analyses.

claim: Constitutive activation of Notch signaling in the lateral line by driving the NICD in transgenic embryos results in deposited neuromasts that are substantially larger than in sibling embryos.
source: When we constitutively activate Notch signaling in the lateral line by driving the NICD in (Tg(cldnB:lynGFP);Tg(cldnB:gal4) x Tg(UAS:nicd)) embryos, we observe that deposited neuromasts are substantially larger than in sibling embryos (Figure 1A–B', Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–A'; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: The NICD transgene is strongly induced when the lateral line placode is forming at 13 hr post fertilization (hpf).
source: The NICD transgene is strongly induced when the lateral line placode is forming at 13 hr post fertilization (hpf) (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments, though the data is not shown.

claim: The NICD transgene is myc-tagged and shows widespread expression in the lateral line and skin.
source: It is also myc-tagged and and shows widespread expression in the lateral line and skin (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The neuromast size increase in NICD embryos is reminiscent of Wnt overexpressing apc mutant neuromasts.
source: The neuromast size increase is reminiscent of Wnt overexpressing apc mutant neuromasts (Figure 1F–F', [Wada et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is a comparison observation supported by figure data and citation.

claim: A reduction of Notch signaling in mib1 mutants causes fragmentation of neuromasts.
source: In contrast, a reduction of Notch signaling in mib1 mutants causes fragmentation of neuromasts (Figure 1E,E'; Video 2; [Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos, and by citation to published literature.

claim: The NICD apical F-actin meshwork is larger compared to wildtype neuromasts, suggesting that NICD neuromasts are composed of more apically constricted cells.
source: Labeling of the first deposited trunk neuromast (L1) with the actin marker phalloidin shows that the NICD apical F-actin meshwork is larger compared to wildtype neuromasts, suggesting that NICD neuromasts are composed of more apically constricted cells (Figure 1G–H').
evidence: This is an inference based on phalloidin staining data shown in the figures.

claim: The robust induction of NICD in transgenic embryos is evidenced by upregulation of the Notch targets notch3 and her4.
source: The robust induction of NICD in (Tg(cldnB:lynGFP);Tg(cldnB:gal4) x Tg(UAS:nicd)) transgenic embryos, is also evidenced by upregulation of the Notch targets notch3, her4, strong activation of the Notch reporter Tp1bglob:EGFP and downregulation of delta ligands (Figure 1I–K' and Figure 1L–N').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: The robust induction of NICD in transgenic embryos is evidenced by strong activation of the Notch reporter Tp1bglob:EGFP.
source: The robust induction of NICD in (Tg(cldnB:lynGFP);Tg(cldnB:gal4) x Tg(UAS:nicd)) transgenic embryos, is also evidenced by upregulation of the Notch targets notch3, her4, strong activation of the Notch reporter Tp1bglob:EGFP and downregulation of delta ligands (Figure 1I–K' and Figure 1L–N').
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in the figures.

claim: The robust induction of NICD in transgenic embryos is evidenced by downregulation of delta ligands.
source: The robust induction of NICD in (Tg(cldnB:lynGFP);Tg(cldnB:gal4) x Tg(UAS:nicd)) transgenic embryos, is also evidenced by upregulation of the Notch targets notch3, her4, strong activation of the Notch reporter Tp1bglob:EGFP and downregulation of delta ligands (Figure 1I–K' and Figure 1L–N').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: In mib1 mutants notch3 and her4 are reduced but not completely absent.
source: On the other hand, in mib1 mutants notch3 and her4 are reduced but not completely absent and delta genes are upregulated (Figure 1I''–J'' and L''–N''; Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures and by citation.

claim: In mib1 mutants delta genes are upregulated.
source: On the other hand, in mib1 mutants notch3 and her4 are reduced but not completely absent and delta genes are upregulated (Figure 1I''–J'' and L''–N''; Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures and by citation.

claim: NICD primordia migrate more slowly than wildtype primordia.
source: NICD primordia migrate more slowly and deposit fewer neuromasts than wildtype primordia and 80% of the NICD primordia do not reach the tail tip, as they deposit too many cells and run out of cells (Figure 1O and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantification shown in the figures.

claim: NICD primordia deposit fewer neuromasts than wildtype primordia.
source: NICD primordia migrate more slowly and deposit fewer neuromasts than wildtype primordia and 80% of the NICD primordia do not reach the tail tip, as they deposit too many cells and run out of cells (Figure 1O and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantification shown in the figures.

claim: 80% of the NICD primordia do not reach the tail tip because they deposit too many cells and run out of cells.
source: NICD primordia migrate more slowly and deposit fewer neuromasts than wildtype primordia and 80% of the NICD primordia do not reach the tail tip, as they deposit too many cells and run out of cells (Figure 1O and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantification shown in the figures, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: During early posterior lateral line development, Notch determines the proportion of placodal cells that contribute to the lateral line ganglion posterior to the ear and how many cells will become part of the migrating primordium.
source: During early posterior lateral line development, Notch determines the proportion of placodal cells that contribute to the lateral line ganglion posterior to the ear and how many cells will become part of the migrating primordium (Mizoguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ectopic activation of Notch signaling generates an initially larger primordium at the expense of the ganglion.
source: Consequently, ectopic activation of Notch signaling generates an initially larger primordium at the expense of the ganglion, which could explain the increase in neuromast size (Figure 1O and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: Primordium size limits how large NICD neuromasts can grow.
source: Indeed primordium size limits how large NICD neuromasts can grow.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NICD neuromasts decrease in size as the primordium becomes smaller during migration.

claim: NICD primordia become increasingly smaller during migration and NICD neuromasts accordingly decrease in size the further posterior they are located along the trunk of the embryo.
source: NICD primordia become increasingly smaller during migration and NICD neuromasts accordingly decrease in size the further posterior they are located along the trunk of the embryo (Figure 1O and P).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: By 32 hpf NICD and sibling primordia consist of the same number of cells but NICD primordia still deposit larger L3 neuromasts.
source: However, by 32 hpf NICD and sibling primordia consist of the same number of cells but NICD primordia still deposit larger L3 neuromasts (Figure 1O and P; Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures and video.

claim: Heat-shock activation of Notch signaling after the primordium and ganglion have separated significantly increases the neuromast cell number.
source: Also, heat-shock activation of Notch signaling after the primordium and ganglion have separated significantly increases the neuromast cell number (Figure 1Q–R', Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from heat-shock experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Although the primordium size determines the maximum size of an enlarged neuromast, the increased NICD neuromast size is independent of the early role of Notch in allocating cells to the primordium.
source: These results indicate that, although the primordium size determines the maximum size of an enlarged neuromast, the increased NICD neuromast size is independent of the early role of Notch in allocating cells to the primordium.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the heat-shock experiments and the observation that NICD neuromasts are larger even when primordium size is the same as siblings.

claim: The size of the migrating primordium is partially controlled by the Hippo pathway components amotl2a and yap1.
source: The size of the migrating primordium is partially controlled by the Hippo pathway components amotl2a (a tight junction-associated scaffolding protein) and yap1 (a transcriptional co-activator) (Agarwala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: amotl2a inhibits proliferation in the primordium.
source: amotl2a inhibits proliferation, whereas yap1 is required in the primordium to reach its normal size.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: yap1 is required in the primordium to reach its normal size.
source: amotl2a inhibits proliferation, whereas yap1 is required in the primordium to reach its normal size.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: yap1 is expressed in the leading 2/3 of the wildtype primordium.
source: yap1 is expressed in the leading 2/3 of the wildtype primordium (Figure 2A') and is upregulated in NICD (Figure 2B').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: yap1 is upregulated in NICD primordia.
source: yap1 is expressed in the leading 2/3 of the wildtype primordium (Figure 2A') and is upregulated in NICD (Figure 2B').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: yap1 is increased in apc primordia correlating with the increased proliferation observed in these embryos.
source: yap1 is also increased in apc primordia correlating with the increased proliferation observed in these embryos (Figure 2D'; [Aman et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data and citation to published literature about proliferation in apc mutants.

claim: yap1 is downregulated in mib1 and Wnt depleted hs:dkk1b primordia.
source: In contrast, yap1 is downregulated in mib1 and Wnt depleted hs:dkk1b primordia (Figure 2C',E').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: yap1 is not expressed in deposited wildtype, NICD, mib1, apc or hs:dkk1b neuromasts suggesting that proliferation in deposited neuromasts is yap1-independent.
source: However, yap1 is not expressed in deposited wildtype, NICD, mib1, apc or hs:dkk1b neuromasts suggesting that proliferation in deposited neuromasts is yap1-independent (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: This is an inference based on in situ hybridization data showing absence of yap1 expression in neuromasts.

claim: The expression of stk3 and amotl2a does not correlate with proliferation in the primordia with manipulated Wnt or Notch signaling.
source: The expression of these genes does not correlate with proliferation in the primordia with manipulated Wnt or Notch signaling, showing that we do not yet fully understand the integration of Hippo signaling with other mitogens and that further studies are needed.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on in situ hybridization data for stk3 and amotl2a shown in supplementary figures.

claim: yap1 morpholino injections inhibit the ectopic proliferation in the primordium that is induced by loss of amotl2a, phenocopying the yap1 mutant.
source: In addition, yap1 morpholino injections inhibit the ectopic proliferation in the primordium that is induced by loss of amotl2a, phenocopying the yap1 mutant (Agarwala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: yap1 morpholino reduces the number of primordium cells in its expression domain in the leading 2/3 of wildtype, apc and NICD primordia.
source: yap1 morpholino reduces the number of primordium cells in its expression domain in the leading 2/3 of wildtype, apc and NICD primordia (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: The decrease in primordium cell number after yap1 morpholino injection is not caused by morpholino-induced p53 activation.
source: The primordium cell number decreases from approximately 100 to 80, which is similar to what we find in yap1 morpholino-injected wildtype embryos (Figure 2H), suggesting that the decrease in cell number is not caused by morpholino-induced p53 activation (Kok et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experiments in p53 mutant embryos showing similar reduction in cell number.

claim: Although yap1 downregulation significantly reduces the size of the primordium, it does not rescue neuromast size in apc or NICD embryos to a wildtype level.
source: Although yap1 downregulation significantly reduces the size of the primordium, it does not rescue neuromast size in apc or NICD embryos to a wildtype level (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: The reduction in NICD L1 and L2 pro-neuromast size in yap1 morphants can be attributed to the role of yap1 in primordium size regulation and that the primordium size limits the number of cells available for allocation into forming neuromast.
source: The reduction in NICD L1 and L2 pro-neuromast size in yap1 morphants (Figure 2F and G) can be attributed to the role of yap1 in primordium size regulation and that the primordium size limits the number of cells available for allocation into forming neuromast (Figure 1O and P).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing correlation between primordium size and neuromast size.

claim: The increase in neuromast size in apc and NICD is yap1 independent.
source: The above experiments show that the increase in neuromast size in apc and NICD is yap1 independent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the yap1 morpholino experiments.

claim: Activation of Wnt signaling produces larger neuromasts via hyperproliferation.
source: Activation of Wnt signaling produces larger neuromasts via hyperproliferation and we therefore tested if proliferation is upregulated in a yap1-independent fashion in NICD primordia and neuromasts (Wada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In contrast to apc neuromasts which show a significant increase in proliferation, NICD neuromasts show a significant decrease.
source: In contrast to apc neuromasts, which show a significant increase in proliferation, NICD neuromasts show a significant decrease (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in the figures.

claim: apc neuromasts gain a significant number of cells after deposition between 32–56 hpf.
source: Accordingly, apc neuromasts gain a significant number of cells after deposition between 32–56 hpf, whereas NICD neuromasts do not significantly grow in cell number (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: NICD neuromasts do not significantly grow in cell number after deposition.
source: Accordingly, apc neuromasts gain a significant number of cells after deposition between 32–56 hpf, whereas NICD neuromasts do not significantly grow in cell number (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: The BrdU index and number of primordium cells in 31 hpf apc primordia is not significantly higher than in the siblings.
source: The BrdU index and number of primordium cells in 31 hpf apc primordia is not significantly higher than in the siblings (Figure 3F,F',H,I), although 33 hpf apc primordia possess a significant increase in proliferating cells (Aman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and cell counting data shown in the figures, with reference to published literature for the 33 hpf time point.

claim: The BrdU index and the number of cells in 35 hpf NICD primordia is unchanged compared to siblings.
source: Similarly, the BrdU index and the number of cells in 35 hpf NICD primordia is unchanged (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation and cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: The striking increase of the BrdU index in deposited apc neuromasts compared to the primordium suggests that apc neuromasts only grow larger once deposited.
source: The striking increase of the BrdU index in deposited apc neuromasts compared to the primordium suggests that apc neuromasts only grow larger once deposited, whereas the increase in the size of NICD neuromasts is controlled by a proliferation-independent process within the primordium, prior to deposition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BrdU incorporation data comparing primordia and neuromasts.

claim: The increase in the size of NICD neuromasts is controlled by a proliferation-independent process within the primordium, prior to deposition.
source: The striking increase of the BrdU index in deposited apc neuromasts compared to the primordium suggests that apc neuromasts only grow larger once deposited, whereas the increase in the size of NICD neuromasts is controlled by a proliferation-independent process within the primordium, prior to deposition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BrdU incorporation data and the observation that NICD neuromasts do not grow after deposition.

claim: The size of the last deposited NICD neuromast is not significantly reduced by cell cycle inhibition, even though the primordium cell number is smaller.
source: Indeed, the size of the last deposited NICD neuromast is not significantly reduced, even though the primordium cell number is smaller (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data after hydroxyurea and aphidicolin treatment shown in the figures.

claim: apc neuromasts were rescued to a wildtype size by cell cycle inhibition and apc primordia became smaller.
source: On the other hand, apc neuromasts were rescued to a wildtype size and apc primordia became smaller (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data after hydroxyurea and aphidicolin treatment shown in the figures.

claim: The induction of Wnt signaling in NICD embryos causes even bigger neuromasts than in untreated NICD embryos, suggesting an additive effect of the two pathways.
source: The induction of Wnt signaling in NICD embryos causes even bigger neuromasts than in untreated NICD embryos, suggesting an additive effect of the two pathways (Figure 3M–O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BIO treatment shown in the figures.

claim: Wnt signaling affects neuromast size via upregulating proliferation in the deposited neuromasts.
source: These results demonstrate that Wnt signaling affects neuromast size via upregulating proliferation in the deposited neuromasts, whereas activation of Notch causes an increase in neuromast size independently of the proliferation rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proliferation assays and cell cycle inhibition experiments.

claim: Activation of Notch causes an increase in neuromast size independently of the proliferation rate.
source: These results demonstrate that Wnt signaling affects neuromast size via upregulating proliferation in the deposited neuromasts, whereas activation of Notch causes an increase in neuromast size independently of the proliferation rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proliferation assays and cell cycle inhibition experiments.

claim: Four cell types have been identified in the primordium: mesenchymal unpatterned cells in the leading region, hair cell precursors, support cells in the center, and future interneuromast cells that are deposited in between neuromasts.
source: As yet, four cell types have been identified in the primordium: (a) mesenchymal, unpatterned cells in the leading region, (b) hair cell precursors, (c) support cells in the center and (d) future interneuromast cells that are deposited in between neuromasts (Figure 1A', arrows).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell types in the primordium.

claim: Interneuromast cells are lateral line stem cells that postembryonically give rise to additional sensory organs.
source: Interneuromast cells are lateral line stem cells that postembryonically give rise to additional sensory organs (Grant et al., 2005; López-Schier and Hudspeth, 2006; Lush and Piotrowski, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the ear and lateral line, Delta/Notch signaling is essential for the specification of sensory hair and support cells.
source: In the ear and lateral line, Delta/Notch signaling is essential for the specification of sensory hair and support cells (Haddon et al., 1999; Itoh and Chitnis, 2001; Riley et al., 1999; Millimaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The deltad-expressing cell differentiates into a hair cell, whereas the surrounding Notch-expressing cells are specified as support cells.
source: The deltad- (and atoh1a) – expressing cell differentiates into a hair cell, whereas the surrounding Notch-expressing cells are specified as support cells (Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: As Notch signaling inhibits atoh1a, NICD neuromasts consist only of support cells.
source: As Notch signaling inhibits atoh1a, NICD neuromasts consist only of support cells (Figure 4A–L).
evidence: This is supported by multiple types of data including SEM, TEM, immunohistochemistry, and in situ hybridization shown in the figures.

claim: Within the primordium only one atoh1a-labeled hair cell precursor exists per proneuromast.
source: However, within the primordium only one atoh1a-labeled hair cell precursor exists per proneuromast (Figure 4K) and their cell fate switch to a support cell cannot account for an increase of an average of 15 or 11 cells in the first proneuromast (orange, Figure 4M–N') and an increase of 12 or 19 cells in the last proneuromast cells at 26 hpf and 30 hpf (green, Figure 4M–N').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data and cell counting shown in the figures.

claim: Hair cell containing neuromasts in heat-shocked Tg(hs:atoh1a;NICD) larvae are not significantly different in size from sibling NICD neuromasts.
source: Hair cell containing neuromasts in heat-shocked Tg(hs:atoh1a;NICD) larvae are not significantly different in size from sibling NICD neuromasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from heat-shock experiments shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The loss of hair cells in NICD neuromasts does not cause the increase in NICD neuromast size.
source: Thus, the loss of hair cells in NICD neuromasts does not cause the increase in NICD neuromast size.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the atoh1a rescue experiments.

claim: hs:atoh1a alone induces a significant increase in neuromast size.
source: Interestingly, hs:atoh1a alone induces a significant increase in neuromast size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C'' and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from heat-shock experiments shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The increase of her4 expression in response to ectopic atoh1a activation suggests that Atoh1a possibly induces larger neuromasts through Notch signaling activation in the primordium.
source: The increase of her4 expression in response to ectopic atoh1a activation suggests that Atoh1a possibly induces larger neuromasts through Notch signaling activation in the primordium (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that her4 is upregulated when atoh1a is activated.

claim: The number of mesenchymal cells in the leading region is initially normal in 26 hpf NICD embryos and is only reduced from an average of 9 to 5 cells in 30 hpf NICD primordia.
source: We determined that the number of mesenchymal cells in the leading region is initially normal in 26 hpf embryos and is only reduced from an average of 9 to 5 cells in 30 hpf NICD primordia (Figure 4M and N').
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: The reduction in the number of leading region cells is insufficient to explain the increase in organ size in NICD embryos.
source: Therefore, the reduction in the number of leading region cells is equally insufficient to explain the increase in organ size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell counting data.

claim: The number of future interneuromast cells is not affected in NICD embryos.
source: The last potential cell fate switch that could contribute to the organ size increase is the loss of future interneuromast cells from the primordium. Future oblong-shaped interneuromast cells are located at the periphery of the primordium (Figure 4M', arrow) but their number is not affected in NICD embryos (Figure 4O–P arrows, Figure 4Q).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in the figures.

claim: The only significant difference detected between NICD and sibling primordia is that NICD primordia possess on average fewer, larger proneuromasts at the expense of a normal-sized proneuromast.
source: The only significant difference we detected between NICD and sibling primordia is that NICD primordia possess on average fewer, larger proneuromasts at the expense of a normal-sized proneuromast (Figure 4M and M', grey cells, and Figure 4R).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting and proneuromast counting data shown in the figures.

claim: Cell fate changes are not major contributors to the increase in organ size in NICD primordia but the allocation of support cells into fewer but larger proneuromasts is the major cause.
source: We therefore conclude that cell fate changes are not major contributors to the increase in organ size in NICD primordia but that the allocation of support cells into fewer but larger proneuromasts is the major cause.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell counting analyses of different cell populations.

claim: The loss of Fgf signaling leads to the loss of proneuromasts/rosettes.
source: The loss of Fgf signaling leads to the loss of proneuromasts/rosettes (Lecaudey et al., 2008; Nechiporuk and Raible, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It has been proposed that the Fgf-expressing central cell in a proneuromast acts as a signaling center that recruits surrounding support cells by inducing Fgf signaling in these cells.
source: It has therefore been proposed that the Fgf-expressing central cell in a proneuromast acts as a signaling center that recruits surrounding support cells by inducing Fgf signaling in these cells (Lecaudey et al., 2008; Nechiporuk and Raible, 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature that the authors test.

claim: Even though fgfr1 is normally expressed in NICD primordia, fgf3, fgf10a and the Fgf targets pea3 and dkk1b are substantially abrogated.
source: Surprisingly, even though fgfr1 is normally expressed, fgf3, fgf10a and the Fgf targets pea3 and dkk1b are substantially abrogated in NICD primordia (Figure 5A,A',B,B',C,C',D,D', Figure 8L,L').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: Fgf signaling is likely reduced in NICD primordia because Notch inhibits atoh1a, which is required for fgf10a expression in the most mature rosettes in the primordium.
source: Fgf signaling is likely reduced because: (a) Notch inhibits atoh1a, which is required for fgf10a expression in the most mature rosettes in the primordium (Figures 4J,L and 5C,C' arrows; [Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010]) and (b) because Notch inhibits Wnt, which normally induces Fgf signaling in the first forming rosette (see below, Figure 8I'–K').
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and published literature about the regulatory relationships.

claim: Fgf signaling is likely reduced in NICD primordia because Notch inhibits Wnt, which normally induces Fgf signaling in the first forming rosette.
source: Fgf signaling is likely reduced because: (a) Notch inhibits atoh1a, which is required for fgf10a expression in the most mature rosettes in the primordium (Figures 4J,L and 5C,C' arrows; [Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010]) and (b) because Notch inhibits Wnt, which normally induces Fgf signaling in the first forming rosette (see below, Figure 8I'–K').
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that Notch inhibits Wnt and that Wnt induces Fgf.

claim: Increased Notch signaling causes decreased Wnt and Atoh1a dependent Fgf signaling.
source: Therefore, increased Notch signaling causes decreased Wnt and Atoh1a dependent Fgf signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the signaling pathway analyses.

claim: The loss of Notch signaling in mib1 mutants leads to loss of Fgf signaling in central cells, however fgfr1a and pea3 are strongly expressed in peripheral cells of the primordium.
source: The loss of Notch signaling in mib1 mutants also leads to loss of Fgf signaling in central cells, however fgfr1a and pea3 are strongly expressed in peripheral cells of the primordium (Figure 5A'',D'').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: In mib1 primordia Fgf signaling is reduced in central cells because of the upregulation of atoh1a, which is normally restricted to a central cell by Notch signaling.
source: In mib1 primordia Fgf signaling is reduced in central cells because of the upregulation of atoh1a, which is normally restricted to a central cell by Notch signaling. Atoh1a, inhibits fgfr1a, thus causing the loss of Fgf signal transduction (Figure 5A''–D''; [Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010]).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and published literature about atoh1a function.

claim: Atoh1a inhibits fgfr1a, thus causing the loss of Fgf signal transduction in mib1 primordia.
source: In mib1 primordia Fgf signaling is reduced in central cells because of the upregulation of atoh1a, which is normally restricted to a central cell by Notch signaling. Atoh1a, inhibits fgfr1a, thus causing the loss of Fgf signal transduction (Figure 5A''–D''; [Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NICD primordia form proneuromasts in the presence of Fgfr1 and MAPK inhibitors.
source: Irrespective of by which method we deplete Fgf signaling in NICD embryos, proneuromasts form, even though the primordium still eventually stalls (Figure 5F',F'',F''',H').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pharmacological inhibitor treatments and heat-shock experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Although the Fgf signal transduction protein di-pErk is absent from Fgf-depleted wildtype and NICD embryos, only in NICD embryos Rock2a and pMRLC are still properly localized to the apical constrictions of proneuromast cells.
source: Also, the molecular analysis of Fgf-depleted wildtype and NICD embryos shows that, although the Fgf signal transduction protein di-pErk is absent from all embryos (Figure 5J'', L''), only in NICD embryos Rock2a and pMRLC are still properly localized to the apical constrictions of proneuromast cells (Figure 5L',P').
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: In the absence of Fgf signaling, Notch signaling is sufficient to apically localize Rock2a and pMRLC and induce/maintain apical constrictions.
source: These results demonstrate that in the absence of Fgf signaling, Notch signaling is sufficient to apically localize Rock2a and pMRLC and induce/maintain apical constrictions (Figure 5I-P').
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunohistochemistry data from Fgf-depleted NICD embryos.

claim: Notch signaling is highly reduced in wildtype siblings in the absence of Fgf signaling but the loss of Fgf signaling has no effect on her4 expression in NICD primordia.
source: Indeed, Notch signaling is highly reduced in the siblings in the absence of Fgf signaling (Figure 5Q–S'; [Nechiporuk and Raible, 2008]) but the loss of Fgf signaling has no effect on her4 expression in NICD primordia (Figure 5R–T').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures and citation to published literature.

claim: Notch acts downstream of the RAS/MAPK pathway.
source: We determined that Notch acts downstream of the RAS/MAPK pathway, as the MAPKK inhibitor PD0325901 leads not only to the loss of the Fgf targets pea3 and fgfr1a but also of notch3 and her4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–F').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data after MAPK inhibitor treatment shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: In the absence of Notch signaling, the activation of Fgf signaling is not sufficient to rescue proneuromast formation.
source: The analysis of the resulting embryos demonstrates that in the absence of Notch signaling, the activation of Fgf signaling is not sufficient to rescue proneuromast formation (Figure 5Y–Y'').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from heat-shock activation of Fgf in mib1 mutants shown in the figures.

claim: The expression of ZO1, a component of the apically localized tight junctions is reduced in mib1;hs:cafgfr1 embryos confirming that Notch acts downstream of Fgf signaling in rosette formation.
source: Also, the expression of ZO1, a component of the apically localized tight junctions is also still reduced in mib1;hs:cafgfr1 embryos (Figure 5Y',Y''') confirming that Notch acts downstream of Fgf signaling in rosette formation.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: shroom3 is an Fgf-dependent scaffolding protein thought to be required for preneuromast cell apical constriction.
source: shroom3 is an Fgf-dependent scaffolding protein thought to be required for preneuromast cell apical constriction (Figure 5U, [Ernst et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is a statement from the literature that the authors test.

claim: shroom3 is lost in Fgf-depleted primordia, reduced in NICD primordia, completely lost in Fgf-depleted NICD primordia and upregulated in mib1 primordia.
source: shroom3 is lost in Fgf-depleted primordia, reduced in NICD primordia, completely lost in Fgf-depleted NICD primordia and upregulated in mib1 primordia (Figure 5U', V, V', W).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: As NICD primordia are forming proneuromasts in the absence of shroom3, shroom3 is not required for rosette formation in the presence of Notch.
source: As NICD primordia are forming proneuromasts in the absence of shroom3 (Figure 5V', arrows), shroom3 is not required for rosette formation in the presence of Notch.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that NICD primordia form rosettes despite lacking shroom3 expression.

claim: Expression of dominant negative shroom3 in wildtype primordia did not cause any rosette or lateral line defects.
source: We also expressed dominant negative shroom3 in wildtype primordia and did not observe any rosette or lateral line defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from dominant negative shroom3 expression shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: shroom3 does not act redundantly with other shroom genes in NICD rosette formation.
source: shroom1 and 2a are not expressed in NICD primordia and we therefore conclude that shroom3 does not act redundantly with other shrooms in NICD rosette formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on in situ hybridization data for shroom family members.

claim: In wildtype primordia Fgfr activation induces Ras-MAPK signaling, which in turn activates Notch signaling.
source: Our results show that in wildtype primordia Fgfr activation induces Ras-MAPK signaling, which in turn activates Notch signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the signaling pathway analyses using inhibitors and genetic manipulations.

claim: Notch leads to the apical localization of Rock2a and pMRLC in a shroom3-independent fashion, leading to apical constriction of the cell.
source: Notch leads to the apical localization of Rock2a and pMRLC in a shroom3-independent fashion, leading to apical constriction of the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunohistochemistry data and shroom3 expression analyses.

claim: Like in wildtype proneuromasts, cells in NICD proneuromasts constrict apically.
source: Like in wildtype proneuromasts, cells in NICD proneuromasts constrict apically (Figure 6A,B,E).
evidence: This is supported by 3D cell shape analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: In 36 hpf mib1 mutant primordia cells in younger proneuromast constrict normally (R2), however cells in the most trailing, about to be deposited rosette (R3) lose apical constrictions and no longer constrict apically.
source: In 36 hpf mib1 mutant primordia cells in younger proneuromast constrict normally (R2), however cells in the most trailing, about to be deposited rosette (R3) lose apical constrictions and no longer constrict apically (Figure 6C–E; Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by 3D cell shape analysis data shown in the figures and video.

claim: mib1 R3 cells are much less constricted than wildtype or NICD R3 cells.
source: We measured cell constrictions in the R3 proneuromast by calculating the ratios between the narrowest cell surface area value by the widest area value. Results confirmed that mib1 R3 cells are much less constricted than wildtype or NICD R3 cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of cell constriction measurements shown in the figures.

claim: The constriction volumes decrease in mib1 as proneuromasts mature and before they are deposited.
source: Subtracting the constriction volumes of R2 from R3 of WT and mib1 proneuromasts reveals that the difference is positive for wildtype proneuromasts, whereas it is negative for mib proneuromasts. Therefore, the constriction volumes decrease in mib1 as they mature and before they are deposited.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of apical constriction volumes shown in the figures.

claim: The disintegration of apical constrictions in mib1 mutants becomes more apparent between 32–36 hpf, as the loss of Notch signaling in mib1 mutants becomes progressively more severe, likely because of depleted maternal stores.
source: The disintegration of apical constrictions becomes more apparent between 32–36 hpf, as the loss of Notch signaling in mib1 mutants becomes progressively more severe, likely because of depleted maternal stores (Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal progression of the phenotype and citation to published literature about maternal contribution.

claim: Transplanted NICD cells do not recruit wildtype cells to contribute to larger neuromasts.
source: We observed that neuromasts only get bigger (green dots) than the average wildtype neuromast (grey line) if they contain NICD clones but not if they contain wildtype clones (Figure 7B). If NICD cells acted as a signaling center enlarged neuromasts should not only contain NICD-positive cells but also possess an above average increase in wildtype cells (black dots). The quantification of all cell transplantation experiments confirmed that the significant increase in neuromast size in NICD>WT experiments (Figure 7B', green bars) is only due to the excessive incorporation of transplanted NICD cells into proneuromasts, as the number of wildtype host cells (black bars) is not significantly changed between two types of cell transplantation strategies. Therefore, we conclude that wildtype cells are not recruited to contribute to larger neuromasts (Figure 7A–B'; Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by cell transplantation experiments and quantification shown in the figures and video.

claim: The increase in organ size after Notch activation is cell-autonomous and Notch transducing cells do not act as a signaling center.
source: Thus, the increase in organ size after Notch activation is cell-autonomous and Notch transducing cells do not act as a signaling center.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell transplantation experiments.

claim: A reduction in e-cadherin expression correlates with lateral line adhesion defects in mib1 mutants.
source: It was suggested that self-organization into rosettes depends on cell adhesion molecules, such as e-cadherin (cdh1) and n-cadherin (cdh2), and a reduction in e-cadherin expression correlates with lateral line adhesion defects in mib1 mutants (Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In NICD primordia e-cadherin mRNA and E-cadherin protein are highly upregulated, accompanied by an increase in the length of adherens junctions in deposited neuromasts.
source: The loss of e-cadherin expression was attributed to the inhibitory effect of the expanded atoh1a domain in mib1 primordia. Correspondingly, we found that in NICD primordia e-cadherin mRNA and E-cadherin protein are highly upregulated, accompanied by an increase in the length of adherens junctions in deposited neuromasts (Figure 7C–C',D–E'',F–H).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization, immunohistochemistry, and quantitative analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Ectopic expression of atoh1a in wildtype primordia causes increased e-cadherin levels and neuromast size.
source: Our data does not support the hypothesis that atoh1a negatively regulates e-cadherin and that therefore the upregulation of e-cadherin could be caused by the loss of atoh1a in NICD primordia. Ectopic expression of atoh1a in wildtype primordia causes increased e-cadherin levels and neuromast size (Figure 7CC'' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from heat-shock atoh1a experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Heat-shock induction of atoh1a leads to the upregulation Notch signaling which induces e-cadherin.
source: Simultaneously, her4 is also induced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and F). These data suggest that heat-shock induction of atoh1a leads to the upregulation Notch signaling which induces e-cadherin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both her4 and e-cadherin are upregulated when atoh1a is activated.

claim: Wnt overexpressing apc mutant primordia show an increase in e-cadherin mRNA and protein expression.
source: Wnt overexpressing apc mutant primordia also show an increase in e-cadherin mRNA and protein expression suggesting that e-cadherin is regulated by Wnt signaling as in many other cell types (Figure 7CC and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B; Heuberger and Birchmeier, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures and citation.

claim: Wnt signaling regulates e-cadherin via the induction of Notch signaling.
source: Our data show that Wnt signaling regulates e-cadherin via the induction of Notch signaling, as e-cadherin is reduced in mib1 primordia and the upregulation of Wnt with the GSK3β inhibitor BIO is not sufficient to induce e-cadherin in Notch-deficient primordia (Figure 7C'' and 7CC').
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from BIO treatment of mib1 mutants shown in the figures.

claim: Fgf signaling indirectly upregulates e-cadherin expression via the induction of Notch signaling.
source: Likewise, Fgf signaling indirectly upregulates e-cadherin expression via the induction of Notch signaling. Loss of Fgf signaling leads to the loss of e-cadherin expression but if Notch is simultaneously activated, e-cadherin is expressed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F').
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from Fgf inhibitor treatment of NICD embryos shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: n-cadherin is regulated by Wnt in a Notch-independent fashion.
source: n-cadherin, on the other hand, is regulated by Wnt in a Notch-independent fashion, as it is not affected in mib1 or NICD primordia (Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010) but it is upregulated in apc mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the supplementary figures and citation.

claim: E-cadherin-deficient cells behave normally in wildtype primordia and neuromasts, even if almost the entire neuromast consists of mutant cells, suggesting that other adhesion molecules act redundantly.
source: E-cadherin-deficient cells behave normally in wildtype primordia and neuromasts, even if almost the entire neuromast consists of mutant cells, suggesting that other adhesion molecules act redundantly (Figure 7—figure supplement 1M–M''; Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by cell transplantation experiments shown in the supplementary figures and video.

claim: Transplanted NICD and wildtype cells contributed equally to either neuromast or interneuromast cell types, demonstrating that cell fate is not affected.
source: First we analyzed if transplanted NICD cells preferentially contribute to neuromast or interneuromast cells and observed that NICD and wildtype cells contributed equally to either lateral line cell type, again demonstrating that cell fate is not affected (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by cell transplantation experiments and quantification shown in the figures.

claim: NICD cells that contribute to interneuromast cells cluster significantly more often than wildtype cells, which are usually aligned in a string.
source: However, NICD cells that contribute to interneuromast cells cluster significantly more often than wildtype cells, which are usually aligned in a string (Figure 7I–I''', arrow and Figure 7K; Figure 7—figure supplement 1N,O).
evidence: This is supported by cell transplantation experiments and quantification shown in the figures.

claim: Almost 76% of NICD cells formed clusters of 2 or more cells, compared to 13% of wildtype cells.
source: Almost 76% of NICD cells formed clusters of 2 or more cells, compared to 13% of wildtype cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell clustering from transplantation experiments.

claim: Notch overexpression changes cell adhesion properties.
source: Combined with the finding that transplanted NICD cells contribute to wildtype neuromasts in larger clusters we conclude that Notch overexpression changes cell adhesion properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell transplantation and clustering data.

claim: 187 genes are upregulated in the lateral line of NICD embryos compared to siblings.
source: We identified 187 genes that are upregulated in the lateral line of NICD embryos (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNASeq analysis data.

claim: GO term analysis revealed that enriched cellular components in NICD lateral line include 'apical junction complex' and 'actin cytoskeleton'.
source: GO term analysis revealed that enriched cellular components are: 'apical junction complex', containing the tight junction components cldnb, cldna, cldne and cingulinb and 'actin cytoskeleton' (Figure 7O–P' and R–S').
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of RNASeq data and in situ hybridization validation shown in the figures.

claim: Upregulated actin cytoskeleton genes in NICD lateral line include formin1 (fmn1), myo5c, baiap2b and cingulinb (cgnb).
source: Upregulated actin cytoskeleton genes are formin1 (fmn1), myo5c, baiap2b and cingulinb (cgnb) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNASeq data shown in source data files and supplementary figures.

claim: cgnb is a tight-junction associated protein that links tight junctions to the actomyosin cytoskeleton and regulates RhoA signaling.
source: cgnb is a tight-junction associated protein that links tight junctions to the actomyosin cytoskeleton and regulates RhoA signaling (Aijaz et al., 2005; Terry et al., 2011; Van Itallie and Anderson, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cingulin function, supported by citations.

claim: Other molecules that interact with the apical junctional complex are also upregulated in NICD lateral line, such as rab25a and celsr2.
source: Other molecules that interact with this complex are also upregulated, such as rab25a, a Rab11 GTPase family member, as is celsr2, an atypical cadherin (Figure 7X–Y').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: Celsr1, if reduced, causes otic defects because of loss of apical constrictions due to disturbed actomyosin recruitment to the apical junctional complex.
source: Celsr1, if reduced, causes otic defects because of loss of apical constrictions due to disturbed actomyosin recruitment to the apical junctional complex (Sai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RNASeq analysis revealed the induction of cd9b by Notch, a Tetraspanin family member implicated in cell-matrix adhesion and Sdf1 (Cxcl12a) mediated migration.
source: RNASeq analysis also revealed the induction of cd9b by Notch, a Tetraspanin family member implicated in cell-matrix adhesion and Sdf1 (Cxcl12a) mediated migration (Figure 7L–M', [Arnaud et al., 2015; Leung et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by RNASeq data and in situ hybridization validation shown in the figures, with citations about cd9b function.

claim: Epithelial cell adhesion molecule (epcam), which regulates claudin expression and tight junctions is strongly upregulated in NICD embryos.
source: By performing in situ hybridization experiments with a number of candidate adhesion molecules, we identified that epithelial cell adhesion molecule (epcam), which regulates claudin expression and tight junctions is also strongly upregulated in NICD embryos (Wu et al., 2013; Figure 7U–V').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures and citation about epcam function.

claim: Molecules induced by NICD are downregulated in mib1 mutants supporting the finding that Notch is regulating the expression of tight junction and adhesion molecules.
source: Conversely, in situ expression analyses demonstrated that molecules induced by NICD are downregulated in mib1 mutants supporting the finding that Notch is regulating the expression of tight junction and adhesion molecules (Figure 7N–Z').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: Cell adhesion is upregulated in NICD cells, as transplanted cells cluster.
source: Our data show that (a) cell adhesion is upregulated in NICD cells, as transplanted cells cluster and (b) cell adhesion molecules act redundantly as their individual downregulation does not cause a phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell transplantation experiments showing clustering.

claim: Cell adhesion molecules act redundantly as their individual downregulation does not cause a phenotype.
source: Our data show that (a) cell adhesion is upregulated in NICD cells, as transplanted cells cluster and (b) cell adhesion molecules act redundantly as their individual downregulation does not cause a phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of phenotypes when individual adhesion molecules are knocked down.

claim: Notch signaling induces an increase in organ size by activating a combination of adherence and tight junction molecules.
source: Given that adhesion and tight junction genes belong to the most highly enriched GO term in NICD primordia, and NICD-positive cells form clusters, we conclude that Notch signaling induces an increase in organ size by activating a combination of adherence and tight junction molecules.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on RNASeq, GO term analysis, and cell behavior observations.

claim: Collective cell migration and organ morphogenesis are coordinated in the primordium via signaling interactions between Wnt and Fgf signaling.
source: Collective cell migration and organ morphogenesis are coordinated in the primordium via signaling interactions between Wnt and Fgf signaling (Aman and Piotrowski, 2008; Chitnis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Wnt signaling in the leading primordium region activates Fgf signaling in the trailing region.
source: Wnt signaling in the leading primordium region activates Fgf signaling in the trailing region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Wnt-Fgf signaling feedback loop.

claim: Both Wnt and Fgf pathways repress the other pathway via the activation of inhibitors in their respective expression domain (dkk1b and sef/dusp6).
source: Both pathways repress the other pathway via the activation of inhibitors in their respective expression domain (dkk1b and sef/dusp6).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Wnt-Fgf signaling feedback loop.

claim: Notch signaling is activated by Fgf signaling in the primordium.
source: Notch signaling is activated by Fgf signaling in the primordium (Figure 5S' and Figure 9A,B; [Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010; Nechiporuk and Raible, 2008]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures and citations to published literature.

claim: Fgf signaling activates the transcription of notch3 in hair cell progenitors and support cells and of atoh1a and delta ligands just in central hair cell progenitors.
source: Fgf signaling activates the transcription of notch3 in hair cell progenitors and support cells and of atoh1a and delta ligands just in central hair cell progenitors (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a summary of the signaling relationships shown in the model figure.

claim: Notch signaling inhibits atoh1 expression.
source: Notch signaling, in turn, inhibits atoh1 expression (Baker et al., 1996; Baker and Yu, 1997; Matsuda and Chitnis, 2010; Millimaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Wnt activates Notch via the activation of Fgf signaling.
source: As Notch is activated by Fgf signaling we asked if Wnt activates Notch via the activation of Fgf signaling. We treated sibling and apc mutants with the Fgfr1 inhibitor PD173074. The loss of Fgf signaling attenuates pea3, atoh1a and her4 in sibling and apc mutants, especially in the youngest proneuromast (Figure 8D–F'), which demonstrates that Wnt signaling is not sufficient to activate either atoh1a or her4 to wildtype levels in the absence of Fgf (Figure 8E,E' and F,F').
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from Fgf inhibitor treatment of apc mutants shown in the figures.

claim: Rosette formation still occurs in NICD primordia with depleted Wnt signaling by heat-shock activation of dkk1b demonstrating that Notch signaling acts downstream of Wnt signaling.
source: Also, rosette formation still occurs in NICD primordia with depleted Wnt signaling by heat-shock activation of dkk1b demonstrating that Notch signaling acts downstream of Wnt signaling (Figure 8G–H').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from heat-shock dkk1b in NICD embryos shown in the figures.

claim: Wnt activates Fgf signaling, which in turn activates atoh1a, delta ligands and Notch signaling.
source: In conclusion, Wnt activates Fgf signaling, which in turn activates atoh1a, delta ligands and Notch signaling (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the signaling pathway analyses shown in the model figure.

claim: In apc primordia the Wnt target wnt10a is not expanded uniformly in the trailing region but is mostly upregulated in a group of central cells suggesting that Wnt signaling is inhibited in more peripheral cells.
source: A clue was provided by our observation that in apc primordia the Wnt target wnt10a is not expanded uniformly in the trailing region but is mostly upregulated in a group of central cells suggesting that Wnt signaling is inhibited in more peripheral cells (Figure 8N,N', arrows).
evidence: This is an inference based on in situ hybridization data shown in the figures.

claim: Notch inhibits wnt10a expression in peripheral cells of the primordium.
source: To test if Notch signaling restricts wnt10a expression in peripheral cells, we treated apc mutant embryos with the γ-secretase and Notch inhibitor DAPT. Indeed, wnt10a is now expressed in the most trailing cells demonstrating that Notch inhibits wnt10a, a feedback interaction not previously described in the primordium (Figure 8O,O').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DAPT treatment of apc mutants shown in the figures.

claim: A Fgf-independent inhibition of Wnt signaling by Notch is supported by the finding that wnt10a expression is still inhibited in NICD primordia treated with Fgf inhibitor.
source: A Fgf-independent inhibition of Wnt signaling by Notch is also supported by our finding that wnt10a expression is still inhibited in NICD primordia treated with Fgf inhibitor, even though loss of Fgf signaling in wildtype embryos leads to expanded wnt10a expression (Figure 8Q–R').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Fgf inhibitor treatment of NICD embryos shown in the figures.

claim: The inhibition of wnt10a by Notch explains why wnt10a is restricted to a single central cell in proneuromast of a wildtype primordium.
source: The inhibition of wnt10a by Notch also explains why wnt10a is restricted to a single central cell in proneuromast of a wildtype primordium (Figure 8M,M').
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing Notch inhibits wnt10a.

claim: Changes in the wnt10a domain only correlate with the presence or absence of Notch (notch3).
source: In conclusion, as illustrated by the schematic representation of gene expression in forming neuromasts, changes in the wnt10a domain only correlate with the presence or absence of Notch (notch3, Figure 8M'–R').
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of wnt10a and notch3 expression patterns under different conditions.

claim: Wnt signaling is normally not only inhibited by the Fgf target dkk1b but also independently by Notch signaling.
source: Thus, the analysis of NICD primordia revealed that Wnt signaling is normally not only inhibited by the Fgf target dkk1b but also independently by Notch signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the signaling pathway analyses.

claim: The loss of Fgf signaling in NICD primordia can be attributed to both the inhibition of Wnt signaling and the inhibition of atoh1a expression by Notch in the trailing region.
source: Therefore, the loss of Fgf signaling in NICD primordia can be attributed to both the inhibition of Wnt signaling and the inhibition of atoh1a expression by Notch in the trailing region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of the signaling relationships.

claim: The conclusion that the loss of Fgf signaling in NICD primordia is mostly caused by Notch-mediated repression of Wnt signaling is confirmed by the finding that Fgf signaling (pea3) can be activated in NICD primordia by activating Wnt signaling with the GSK3β inhibitor BIO.
source: The conclusion that the loss of Fgf signaling in NICD primordia is mostly caused by Notch-mediated repression of Wnt signaling is confirmed by our finding that Fgf signaling (pea3) can be activated in NICD primordia by activating Wnt signaling with the GSK3β inhibitor BIO (Figure 8S,S').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BIO treatment of NICD embryos shown in the figures.

claim: Notch is a component of the Wnt/Fgf signaling interaction network that controls migration with organ morphogenesis.
source: Combined our pathway analyses revealed that Notch is a component of the Wnt/Fgf signaling interaction network that controls migration with organ morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the comprehensive signaling pathway analyses.

claim: Wnt signaling upregulates proliferation in deposited neuromasts.
source: Wnt signaling upregulates proliferation in deposited neuromasts, whereas Notch signaling induces an increase in organ size as they form within the primordium in a proliferation-independent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on BrdU incorporation assays and cell cycle inhibition experiments.

claim: Cell cycle inhibition in NICD embryos does not rescue the neuromast size, in line with previous study that demonstrated that proliferation does not influence wildtype neuromast size.
source: Accordingly, cell cycle inhibition in NICD embryos does not rescue the neuromast size, in line with our previous study that demonstrated that proliferation does not influence wildtype neuromast size (Aman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cell cycle inhibition experiments and citation to previous work.

claim: Although inhibition of the Hippo pathway component amotl2a causes an increase in proliferation in the primordium and yap1 morpholino injections reduce the primordium size, neither manipulation affects the size of the forming sensory organs in wildtype, apc or NICD embryos.
source: Likewise, although inhibition of the Hippo pathway component amotl2a causes an increase in proliferation in the primordium (Agarwala et al., 2015) and yap1 morpholino injections reduce the primordium size, neither manipulation affects the size of the forming sensory organs in wildtype, apc or NICD embryos (Figure 2G–H; [Agarwala et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures and citation to published literature.

claim: Primordium size and lateral line organ size are regulated by independent mechanisms.
source: Thus, primordium size and lateral line organ size are regulated by independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the yap1 experiments showing that primordium size changes do not affect neuromast size.

claim: In amotl2a mutant embryos on average one more neuromast develops.
source: However, in amotl2a mutant embryos on average one more neuromast develops (Agarwala et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Primordium size does not affect neuromast size in a wildtype embryo but rather affects neuromast number.
source: Thus, primordium size does not affect neuromast size in a wildtype embryo but rather affects neuromast number.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that amotl2a mutants have more neuromasts but not larger neuromasts.

claim: yap1 is upregulated and amotl2a is reduced by Notch signaling without affecting the primordium cell number suggesting that yap1 also possesses proliferation-independent functions that need to be further explored.
source: yap1 is upregulated and amotl2a is reduced by Notch signaling without affecting the primordium cell number suggesting that yap1 also possesses proliferation-independent functions that need to be further explored (Figures 3H–I, 9A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that yap1 is upregulated but proliferation is not increased in NICD primordia.

claim: RNASeq and GO term analyses of FACS isolated primordium cells revealed that members of the epithelial junctional complex are upregulated in the lateral line of NICD embryos.
